lede: A grain merchant's son who was meant to be a lawyer, picked up a box of paints while lying ill in bed at twenty, and spent the next sixty years finding out how far colour alone could carry a picture.

ps: Henri Matisse was born on 31 December 1869 in Le Cateau-Cambresis, in northern France, and grew up in the nearby town of Bohain-en-Vermandois, where his father sold grain and seed.

In 1905 his pictures of flat, burning colour caused a scandal in Paris and gave a name, the Fauves or 'wild beasts', to a new movement. He became, with Picasso, one of the two artists who most shaped painting in the 20th century.
After major surgery in 1941 he worked mostly from a bed or wheelchair, 'drawing with scissors' in painted paper. He designed a whole chapel at Vence and died in Nice on 3 November 1954, aged 84.
He was the eldest son and expected to take over the family business. Instead he studied law in Paris and became a clerk in a lawyer's office in Saint-Quentin, copying documents.

ps.t: In 1890, recovering from appendicitis, he was given a box of paints by his mother to pass the time. He later said that from then on he felt he had found a kind of paradise.

ps: In 1891 he gave up the law and went to Paris. He studied at the Academie Julian and then with the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau, who encouraged his pupils to think for themselves. He also spent long hours copying old masters in the Louvre.
His early pictures were dark and careful. In the late 1890s, after seeing Impressionist painting and the light of Brittany and Corsica, his colours began to brighten.
1899: though very short of money, he bought a small Cezanne painting of bathers from the dealer Ambroise Vollard. He kept it for 37 years as a lesson in structure, then gave it to the city of Paris.
Summer 1904: at Saint-Tropez with the painter Paul Signac he tried painting in small dots of pure colour. The result was Luxe, calme et volupte.

Summer 1905: at Collioure, a fishing port near Spain, he and Andre Derain painted with unmixed colours straight from the tube, letting colour stand for light and feeling rather than copying what they saw.

Autumn 1905: their pictures hung together at the Salon d'Automne. Visitors laughed at Matisse's Woman with a Hat, a portrait of his wife with a face of green, mauve and orange. The American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein bought it.
1906: at the Steins' apartment in Paris he met the young Pablo Picasso. Matisse's large Joy of Life of that year was one of the paintings Picasso answered with Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.

1909 to 1910: the Moscow merchant Sergei Shchukin commissioned two huge panels for his house, Dance and Music. Five red figures dance in a ring against blue and green. The panels are now in the Hermitage in St Petersburg.
1911: he painted The Red Studio, his own studio drowned in one flat red, with his works floating inside it. It is now at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
1917: he began spending most of each year in Nice, painting sunlit rooms, open windows and models posed as odalisques.
1941: in Lyon he had an operation for cancer of the abdomen and nearly died. He called the years that followed his second life.
1948 to 1951: he designed the Chapel of the Rosary at Vence, from its stained glass and wall drawings to the priests' robes. It was consecrated in June 1951.
Woman with a Hat (1905). The picture that launched Fauvism: a portrait in which nothing is the 'right' colour, and everything holds together.
Dance (1909 to 1910). Five red figures on a hill of green under a blue sky, painted in just three colours, swinging round in a ring.
The Red Studio (1911). An interior in which walls, floor and furniture all vanish into a single red, so the paintings on the walls become the subject.
Jazz (1947). A book of brightly coloured stencil prints made from cut paper, with pages of his handwritten thoughts.

Blue Nudes (1952) and The Snail (1953). Late cut-outs, cut from sheets painted with gouache and pinned to the wall by his assistants under his direction. The Snail, almost three metres across, is in Tate Modern in London.

ps.t: In his essay Notes of a Painter (1908) he said he dreamed of an art of balance and serenity, something like a good armchair for a tired mind.

ps: Amelie Parayre (1872 to 1958), his wife from 1898, who supported the family with a hat shop in their poorest years and posed for Woman with a Hat. They separated in 1939.

Marguerite Matisse (1894 to 1982), his daughter from an earlier relationship with Caroline Joblau, raised in the family. In 1944 she was arrested and tortured by the Gestapo for her work in the Resistance and survived. His sons were Jean (1899) and Pierre (1900), who became an art dealer in New York.
Pablo Picasso (1881 to 1973), his great rival and friend. They traded paintings in 1907 and visited each other in old age.
Paul Cezanne (1839 to 1906), the painter he called 'the father of us all', according to later reports.
Gertrude Stein (1874 to 1946), the American writer who, with her brothers, was among his first serious collectors.
Lydia Delectorskaya (1910 to 1998), a Russian refugee who became his studio assistant in the 1930s, then his model and manager until his death.

Paris from 1900 to 1914 was the centre of the art world. In a few years Fauvism, Cubism and abstraction followed one another, and collectors from Russia and America, like Shchukin and the Steins, bought what French museums would not.
Both world wars reached his family. In 1940 he refused a chance to leave France for Brazil. His wife and daughter were both arrested in 1944 for Resistance work.
He showed that colour could be the main subject of a painting, not only its decoration. Abstract painters in America, such as Mark Rothko, looked closely at works like The Red Studio.
The Matisse Museum in Nice and the Matisse Museum in Le Cateau-Cambresis, which he founded himself in 1952, hold large collections. The Vence chapel can still be visited.

myths.t: The name came from the critic Louis Vauxcelles. Seeing a classical-style sculpture in the same room as the bright paintings in 1905, he wrote of 'Donatello among the wild beasts'. The painters never formed a club, and the movement lasted only about three years.

myths.c: Matisse and Picasso hated each other.
myths.t: They were rivals who watched each other closely for fifty years and borrowed from each other. Picasso is reported to have said that only Matisse truly understood him. In old age they visited and exchanged pictures.

myths.c: He made cut-outs because he could no longer paint.
myths.t: He had used cut paper to plan the Barnes Foundation mural in the early 1930s, long before his illness. After the 1941 surgery he found it easier to work from his bed or chair with assistants, and he chose cut-outs as a new art, not a fallback. He still drew and painted in the 1940s.
That was what some critics said in 1905. He had years of academic training, copied old masters and worked slowly; Woman with a Hat went through many changes.
